cards.title: COP collapse
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: This matters for understanding global climate policy failures, international relations, and the urgent impacts of climate change, vital for Current Affairs and Environment topics.
cards.summary: Climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya recently failed to reach a deal, making it the first conference without an agreement since 2009. The primary reasons for this collapse were disagreements over phasing out fossil fuels, resisted by petro-states, and a lack of commitment to climate finance for vulnerable countries. This failure highlights a global unwillingness to cooperate, even as severe climate impacts like glacier collapses, heatwaves, and wildfires intensify worldwide. The urgency of climate action is increasing with nature showing 'unrelenting' impacts.
key_facts: COP31 climate negotiations recently collapsed in Antalya.
This was the first climate conference to end without a deal since the 2009 Copenhagen Summit.
A key reason for failure was the omission of phasing out fossil fuels from the draft agreement due to pressure from petro-states like Saudi Arabia and Russia.
The EU, Britain, and some climate-vulnerable states rejected this omission.
Another issue was the lack of commitment to providing climate finance for poor, vulnerable countries.
Nepal recently experienced a massive glacier collapse, causing floods and hundreds of deaths, while Europe saw over 50,000 heatwave deaths last summer.

vocab.meaning: firmly established and difficult to change

text: THE collapse of climate negotiations at COP31 in Antalya recently is a stark reminder of a world disinclined to cooperate for the common good. The first climate conference to end without a deal since the 2009 Copenhagen Summit, COP31 succumbed to entrenched divisions among the delegates.

The main sticking point was the phasing out of fossil fuels , which was not mentioned in the draft agreement because of pressure from the petro-states including Saudi Arabia and Russia. This omission was rejected by the EU, Britain, and some small, climate-vulnerable states, which rightly hold fossil fuels responsible for global warming. Another stumbling block was the lack of commitment to providing climate finance.

Ironically, many of the countries that opposed the deal for not including the transition away from fossil fuels, refused to move forward on earlier pledges to provide and mobilise funding for poor climate-vulnerable countries. It has been noted, in fact, that many of the latter prefer funds over curbs on fossil fuels at this stage, given their need to rehabilitate lives already impacted by climate change and build infrastructure strong enough to withstand future shocks. This may have been one reason why some vulnerable countries curtailed their objections to the draft deal.

Day by day, the climate question is assuming greater urgency. Indeed, nature has been unrelenting against the backdrop of COP31. While Pakistan was largely spared the onrush of swelling rivers this year, Nepal witnessed a tragedy when a massive glacier collapse led to the flooding of vast tracts of land, killing hundreds. Heatwaves in Europe reportedly killed over 50,000 people last summer, while wildfires in Spain and France forced thousands of families from their homes.

“Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C raises the risk of irreversible changes […] along with devastating human impacts,” warns the UN’s main environmental agency in its latest Emissions Gap report. The need for cooperation and consensus on tackling climate change has never been greater.

Luckily, the failure of COP31 does not spell the end of climate diplomacy. International regimes built over years to combat a danger that knows no borders are too far advanced to come undone because an agreement was not reached in Antalya. But time is running out.

Given national interests and the nature of geopolitics, absolute consensus may be hard to forge. However, smaller regional initiatives, where countries — especially of the developing world — share green technology and other climate-friendly solutions can be pursued. These countries — which pollute the least but bear the brunt of global warming — have every right to ask for funds from the world’s chief polluters. The question is whether they have the will to safeguard their future through collective action.

cards.title: Civilisational dialogue
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: This highlights the state of Pakistan-India relations, the role of multilateral forums in diplomacy, and the potential for dialogue despite strained ties, crucial for Pakistan Affairs and International Relations.
cards.summary: Pakistan's Climate Change Minister, Musadik Malik, recently attended the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi, a significant development given the current lack of bilateral engagement between Pakistan and India. Although no major breakthrough was expected, such multilateral meetings offer a chance for informal discussions and can help reduce regional tensions. The minister highlighted climate change as a common regional threat and skillfully handled media questions on 'terrorism' and the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), emphasizing Pakistan's own concerns. Such engagements are seen as crucial for lowering confrontational rhetoric as there is no viable alternative to peace in South Asia.
key_facts: Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik recently visited New Delhi.
He attended the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, a multilateral meeting.
Bilateral engagement between Pakistan and India is currently very limited due to New Delhi’s rigidity.
The minister highlighted climate change as a common threat to the South Asian region.
He addressed Indian media questions regarding 'terrorism' and the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT).
Pakistan also has concerns that it would address if India initiated discussions on irritants.

vocab.meaning: a comment or statement that is often repeated

text: WHENEVER representatives of Pakistan and India meet, even in multilateral settings, there is hope for a rekindling of ties. This is so because bilateral engagement is currently close to zero, mainly because of New Delhi’s rigidity. But considering last year’s armed conflict between both states, and the ensuing toxic atmosphere in South Asia, it is a welcome development that Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik travelled to New Delhi recently for the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum.

This was a multilateral meeting and there were no great expectations of a bilateral breakthrough attached to the visit. But the fact that it took place at all despite the state of ties is significant. Sometimes at such events, behind closed doors, representatives of both states can discuss small steps to improve relations.

Mr Malik brought up the issue of climate change threatening the whole region, while highlighting the common civilisational bonds that tie South Asia and Eurasia together — bonds which have unfortunately become hostage to the rigidity of some, particularly in the subcontinent. The minister also deserves praise for deftly handling pointed questions from the Indian media about ‘terrorism’ — apparently New Delhi’s favourite refrain when it comes to Pakistan — as well as the IWT. Mr Malik said that he was in India for an SCO event; when the Indians would call him to discuss terrorism and other irritants, he would address these specifically, as Pakistan also had concerns.
Though there are no signs of the deep freeze in bilateral relations thawing anytime soon, engagements such as these can help bring down the temperature, and lower confrontational rhetoric.

The fact is there is no viable alternative to peace in South Asia, and only through a structured dialogue can both states address their concerns satisfactorily, and work towards a more peaceful future for all.

Of course the Indian side must stop issuing threats to Pakistan, and using adversarial language. While Pakistan has defended itself against Indian aggression in the past, and will do so again if threatened, the subcontinent’s people deserve to live in peace, not eternal conflict.
When India is ready to engage Pakistan in a civil, frank and respectful dialogue, it will find this country ready to respond.

cards.title: Space for culture
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: This topic explores the role of culture in national integration, public education, and social cohesion, which is relevant for Pakistan Affairs, National Integration, and Governance essays.
cards.summary: Karachi recently hosted the World Culture Festival by the Arts Council of Pakistan, a large 25-day event featuring over 1,000 artists from more than 150 countries. Such cultural festivals are powerful tools for uniting people, fostering harmony, and bridging societal divides like class, language, and ethnicity within Pakistan. The government should encourage more similar initiatives, especially in smaller cities, and reduce bureaucratic hurdles to ensure broader public participation and interaction among diverse groups. These platforms are crucial for collective societal progress and for citizens to engage with policymakers and celebrated figures, especially when the country faces significant challenges.
key_facts: The World Culture Festival by the Arts Council of Pakistan recently concluded in Karachi.
It was a 25-day event featuring over 1,000 artists from more than 150 countries.
Artistic expression can bind people, build consensus, and forge harmony between nations.
Cultural platforms can help bridge internal chasms of class, language, and ethnicity in Pakistan.
There is a need for more such events, especially in smaller cities, and reduced bureaucratic hurdles.

vocab.meaning: an elaborate and spectacular entertainment or production
profound differences between people, viewpoints, feelings, or things
levels or classes into which people in a society are grouped

text: AS winter arrives, cultural and literary festivals get set to pull together talents from across the country and the world. The first extravaganza of the season was the World Culture Festival by the Arts Council of Pakistan. An impressive 25-day affair, comprising over 1,000 artists from more than 150 countries, it came to a close over the weekend. An entertainment-starved Karachi became the venue for approximately 200 performances. This is quite a feat. Indeed, artistic expression, preferably unrestrained, is a tool more powerful than even social media to bind people, build consensus, forge harmony and strong relations between nations. Pakistan can do with a variety of similar platforms not just to present a united image but also to bridge the internal chasms of class, language and ethnicity.

Undoubtedly, fairs, concerts, fervent debates and conferences of all types are popular means to engage and educate the citizenry. Yet there are not many of them, and fewer still in smaller cities. In fact, the elitist nature of certain events ensures that they operate in silos, separate from the larger public. As the populace writhes in economic pain, the government could do more to provide avenues of relief and cultural interaction. Shared culture requires investment and reduced bureaucratic hurdles for all strata of society to interact with participants from other regions. With the country at an extraordinary crossroads, these platforms become all the more necessary as spaces where people can ponder over ways to achieve a better collective future from varied perspectives. Crucially, common citizens should get the opportunity to brush shoulders with celebrated names and policymakers so they are able to know their views, and to air their own. For this, organisers must ensure inclusive gatherings involving the youth for new ideas, and themes that prioritise the humanities, history, heritage, and literature. Lastly, political discussions, along with favouritism on panels, must take a back seat.
